bioghist.head: Lucien Aigner (1901-1999)
bioghist.p: Lucien Aigner was a Jewish-born Hungarian photojournalist most known for his photographs of notable figures such as Louis Armstrong, Winston Churchill, Albert Einstein, Adolf Hitler, Benito Mussolini, Norman Rockwell, and Emperor Haile Selassie. Born on September 14, 1901, in Érsekújvár, Austria-Hungary (now Nové Zámky in Slovakia), Aigner briefly studied theater in Berlin, where he worked as an assistant camera operator to Stefan Lorant, a lifelong friend and influential filmmaker. He earned a degree in law from the University of Budapest in 1924 and converted from Judaism to Protestantism at some point during his education. After graduation, Aigner became a reporter and photographer for Az Est , the Hungarian newspaper group. He relocated to Paris in 1925 and operated as the Paris correspondent of the London General Press at the Stresa Conference of 1935. There, Aigner captured an image of Mussolini as he was about to sneeze; the photograph made the cover of Newsweek and established Aigner as a photojournalist. Aigner was among the early adopters of the 35mm Leica camera, which he used from 1925 to 1938. He began using a Rolleiflex camera in 1939. The same year, Aigner and his family emigrated from France to the United States to escape Nazi persecution. In the late 1940s and early 1950s, he worked as an announcer, producer, and director for Voice of America radio, while continuing to do freelance photojournalism. He also produced several documentary films. In 1953, Aigner established a portrait studio in Great Barrington, Massachusetts, which he operated until 1977. In later years of his life, Aigner focused on cataloging and indexing his large collection of negatives and exhibiting his photographs in the United States and Europe. He died in Waltham, Massachusetts in 1999.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: The collection contains contact sheets, negatives, transparencies, slides, photographic prints, scrapbooks, writings, professional and personal papers, correspondence, printed material, cameras and other recording equipment, and audiovisual and computer media created and collected by Hungarian photojournalist Lucien Aigner.

Photographic materials document historical events in the 1930s and 1940s, such as the 1932 Geneva Conference for the Reduction and Limitation of Armaments, Stresa Conference of 1935, the 1936 Berlin Olympics, and the 1945 United Nations Conference on International Organization in San Francisco. Other subjects include Coney Island and Harlem, New York; ballet dancers practicing at the Ope?ra de Paris; Jardin du Luxembourg in Paris; Bastille Day in Paris; and the marriage of King Zog I of Albania. Notable figures in the collection include Louis Armstrong, Josephine Baker, Winston Churchill, Marlene Dietrich, Albert Einstein, Mahatma Gandhi, Adolf Hitler, Fiorello H. La Guardia, Stefan Lorant, Lorin Maazel, Guglielmo Marconi, Yehudi Menuhin, Benito Mussolini, Norman Rockwell, Sara Delano Roosevelt, William Saroyan, Haile Selassie, and Harry S. Truman. The collection additionally contains portraits taken at Aigner's Great Barrington studio, his series of New York child portraits, and photographs of schools, camps, and churches.
Writings contain photo stories, drafts and materials related to published and planned books, diaries, and radio and play scripts by Aigner.

Correspondence concerns business and personal matters and includes letters from Helen Dukas, Stefan Lorant, Lorin Maazel, Norman Rockwell, and Sara Delano Roosevelt, as well as third party exchanges between Aigner's family members and others.

Papers include inventories and descriptions of photographs and other material in the collection, created by Aigner as he cataloged his work in the 1970s to 1990s; files related to exhibitions, research, projects, and Aigner's portrait studio work in Great Barrington; business and financial records; and personal and family papers. Printed material includes books, catalogs, clippings, magazines, pamphlets, postcards, posters, and other ephemera by or relating to Aigner.
Printed material includes books, catalogs, clippings, magazines, pamphlets, postcards, posters, and other ephemera by or relating to Aigner.
Also included are objects and photographic equipment, such as Aigner's studio stamps, one Kodak Brownie box camera, two Graflex press cameras, and a Bell and Howell motion picture camera.

Audiovisual and computer media consists of reel-to-reel film, audio and videocassettes, floppy disks, and CDs and DVDs. Audiovisual material includes interviews of Aigner, recordings relating to his exhibitions, the documentary "Life with the Camera," and Aigner's film about educator and missionary Frank Laubach.
Printed material transferred from Acquisitions consists of printed items that were reviewed and deemed to be returned to the collection.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: This series consists of photographic prints, negatives, transparencies, slides, and contact sheets primarily depicting political events; European and American social life, music, arts, dance, film, and theater; children and education; and religion. Also included are materials related to exhibitions of Lucien Aigner's work and related books. Most photographs dating in the 1930s are candid shots from New York, Paris, and other European locations, created with a 35-millimeter Leica camera. Among the images captured during this era are Mussolini about to sneeze at the Stresa Conference of 1935; Nazi Party marches and Hitler at the 1936 Olympics; political meetings of Communists and Socialists; European, British, and American politicians; scenes from Harlem, Coney Island, and Rikers Island Penitentiary photographed during a 1936 trip to New York; and celebrity portraits. Photographs dating from 1939 to 1955 were made with a Rolleiflex (2 ¼ x 2 ¼ size) and feature personalities such as Albert Einstein, figure skater Sonja Henie, New York Mayor Fiorello La Guardia, Soviet ambassador Maxim and Ivy Litvinov, musician Lorin Maazel, Sara Delano Roosevelt, and Chinese diplomat and scholar Hu Shih; New York schools and schoolchildren; prayer and churches; the National Music Camp in Michigan; and the 1945 United Nations charter conference in San Francisco. Photographs after 1955 include portraits created in Aigner's Great Barrington studio and photographs from Aigner's travels in Europe and in Hong Kong with missionary Frank Laubach.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: This subseries consists of black-and-white vintage and non-vintage prints of various sizes documenting Aigner's career as a photojournalist and photographs by others of Aigner and his family. Vintage photographs, printed from original negatives close to the time of film exposure, measure 7 by 10 inches and smaller and feature photo agency stamps on the verso. Some contain Aigner's original captions. Photographs measuring 8 by 10 inches and larger are generally test prints or non-vintage prints created later by Aigner or his assistants, Arthur Gerstein and John Snyder. Later prints of vintage subjects often contain crop marks and notations related to exposure for future printing, including photographs created for the International Center of Photography's 1979 Aigner publication and exhibition. The subseries also contains large-format prints, generally measuring from 14 by 18 inches to 20 by 24 inches, used in exhibitions such as Aigner's New York , Aigner's Paris 50 Years Later , and the 50th anniversary of the United Nations.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: This subseries contains original and copy negatives, transparencies, and slides of vintage prints by Aigner, as well as images of exhibitions and book layouts. Included are 35-millimeter black-and-white negatives, transparencies, and slides, and negatives and transparencies measuring 2 ¼ by 2 ¼ inches and 4 by 5 inches. The collection also contains some color negatives and slides. Many of the negatives depicting French life and culture are copies of originals held by the Bibliothèque nationale de France. Aigner partnered with Polaroid Corporation to copy select 35mm negatives onto Polaroid Type 55 positive/negative film, which were used to make new prints for the Aigner's Paris exhibition and catalog in 1982. Also present are boxes in which Aigner stored rolled original negatives from the 1930s in individual compartments, with handwritten indexes on the interior box lids.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Photo stories consist of illustrated articles written by Aigner from the 1930s to 1970s. Materials include drafts of articles and captions written by Aigner or his collaborators in English, French, or Hungarian; accompanying photographs taken by Aigner or collected by him from other sources; and related notes, correspondence, research material, and clippings. Photo stories from the 1930s frequently depict Paris life, and also feature Saint-Cyr, Quai d'Orsay, travels to Albania, Bulgaria, Switzerland, and a visit to New York depicting Harlem, Coney Island, and Rikers Island Penitentiary. After immigrating to the United States in 1939, Aigner continued to produce photo stories for publications such as The Christian Science Monitor , Click , and Popular Photography . Subjects from 1939 to the 1950s include New York schools, summer camps, gifted children, World War II-era social programs, the National Music Camp, the 1945 United Nations Charter Conference in San Francisco, and the Roosevelts' Hyde Park estate. Later photo stories cover the Experiment in International Living program and locations throughout Massachusetts. Notable personalities featured in photo stories include Albert Einstein, diplomats Maxim Litvinov and Hu Shih, conductor Lorin Maazel, violinist Yehudi Menuhin, artist Norman Rockwell, Sara Delano Roosevelt, and King Zog I of Albania. Also present are nine scrapbooks of clipped photo stories compiled by Aigner.

scopecontent.p: This subseries consists of notes, drafts, correspondence, research material, and subject files pertaining to Aigner's photography projects, films, and other creative endeavors. Photography projects include commercial catalogs of Aigner's work, such as a portfolio of Albert Einstein portraits; a collaboration with Polaroid Corporation to transfer his vintage negatives onto Polaroid film; and pictorial records of New York schoolchildren.

Aigner's works about missionary Frank Laubach include articles, a planned biography, and his documentary film Hong Kong Breakthrough ; material consists of drafts and scripts, clippings, and collected photographs of Laubach and family. Also present are planning files for Aigner's short film Paintings for Halloween and the 1987 documentary Lucien Aigner: A Life with the Camera , and transcripts of an oral history project. Research and project files frequently include photographic prints.
